nodes.question: What was the relationship between economic growth and environmental quality found in the study?
nodes.answer: Economic growth improves environmental quality, according to the findings of the study.
nodes.paragraph: Transitioning to sustainable energy and enhanced environmental quality in Somalia through renewable energy, globalisation and trade openness Abdikafi Hassan Abdi1,2 , Abdimalik Ali Warsame2, Mohamed Okash Sugow1 & Hassan Abdikadir Hussein3 A balanced approach that combines trade policies, renewable energy promotion, and robust environmental regulations is crucial for improving ecological sustainability. Although the literature suggests that trade openness facilitates the transfer of cleaner energy technologies to developing nations, existing empirical studies have produced inconclusive results, particularly in Somalia S context. Therefore, this study explores the dynamic relationships between renewable energy, trade openness, economic growth, globalisation, and environmental degradation using annual time-series data from 1990 to 2019. Employing advanced econometric methods, including the autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) model and dynamic OLS analyses, the findings reveal significant long-run cointegration among the variables. The essential insights of this study affirm that renewable energy strengthens environmental quality in both the short- and long-run, which stipulates its potential as a sustainable solution for Somalia. Conversely, trade openness has a detrimental impact on environmental quality in both the short- and long-run. While globalisation hinders environmental quality in the short-run, economic growth improves it.

nodes.question: How has the environmental goods sector performed compared to the overall economy in the European Union from 2000 to 2020?
nodes.answer: The environmental goods sector in the European Union has grown at an average annual growth rate of 3.4%, while the GDP grew by only 1.0% on average per year during that period.
nodes.paragraph: The environmental goods sector has grown more rapidly than the overall economy of countries. nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Decent work and economic growth|Economic stability|Economic growth_qna_002
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What is the traditional measure of economic growth often used by countries?
nodes.answer: The traditional measure of economic growth used by countries is gross domestic product (GDP).
nodes.paragraph: Traditionally, gross domestic product (GDP) has been used as a measure of economic growth, and ultimately, as the main indicator of societal progress and success for many countries [5 ]. GDP measures the total monetary or market value of goods and services produced within a country within a specific time period (typically at annual time intervals). Using GDP statistics as a measure of soci- etal success is increasingly being viewed as problematic by prominent economists, social commentators and govern- ments of the member countries of the WEAII, as it fails to consider the negative effects created in the process of production and development of ever-increasing volumes of goods and services, including e.g., over-population; pollution and erosion of the natural environment; climate change and biodiversity loss [6 ]. A wellbeing economy starts with the idea that the economy should serve people and communities first and foremost, rather than a traditional economic model, which assumes that a successful economy will lead to a success- ful society. Hence, it is based on a new and different vision of societal progress co-created through engagement with communities about what matters most for their collective wellbeing [2 4].

nodes.question: According to the literature review, what are some negative effects of economic growth?
nodes.answer: Negative effects of economic growth include increased carbon emissions, global warming, and other forms of pollution.

nodes.question: How is economic activity represented in the studies referenced by Bennedsen et al. (2021)?
nodes.answer: Economic activity is represented by common factors extracted from a large set of annual macroeconomic US variables.
nodes.paragraph: Furthermore, using the nonlinear factor-augmentedregression proposed by Bai and Ng ( 2008 ), he concludes that the polynomial terms of the factors are not signi cant and, therefore, the EKC is not found in the short run. More recently, Bennedsen et al. ( 2021 ) propose a structural augmented dynamic factor model (SADFM) for annual CO 2emissions in the US. As in Fosten ( 2019 ), the economic activity is represented by common factors, which are extracted from a large set of annual macroeconomic US variables using the two-step Kalman Iter (2SKF) procedure of Doz et al. ( 2011 ) instead of PC. The SADFM also includes additional explanatory variables selected from the same set of economic variables byusing procedures based on Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) of Tibshirani ( 1996 ), Elastic Nets (EN) of Zou and Hastie ( 2005 ) and Autometrics of Doornik ( 2009 ) and Doornik and Hendry ( 2009 ). They conclude that, once the selected explanatory variables, in particular, Industrial Production (IP), are included in the model, the explanatory power of the factors is negligible.
